newsitem.title: UK: Energy bid talks spark other sector shares.
newsitem.headline: Energy bid talks spark other sector shares.

text.p: A possible bid for electricity and coal company The Energy Group plc from U.S.-based PacifiCorp sent power shares higher on Wednesday as the market contemplated the first bid in the sector under the gaze of the new Labour government.
Energy Group, Britain's biggest electricity distributor, said after the market closed on Tuesday that it was in talks with PacifiCorp which could lead to a merger through a recommended cash offer.

It said any offer would be expected to be priced at about a 20 percent premium to its closing share price on Tuesday of 580 pence, which already valued it at around three billion pounds ($4.9 billion).
Energy Group shares surged higher to reach 672 pence on Wednesday morning but later eased off highs to be up 70 pence at 650 pence per share by 1210 GMT.
"A bid around seven pounds per share would be reasonable, possibly a touch higher," said one analyst who declined to be named.
Other shares in the sector were pushed higher, with regional electricity company (Rec) Southern Electric up 14 pence to 430 pence and generator Scottish Hydro gaining 18.5 pence to 419 pence.
"The big news is that the Americans are back," said Yamaichi utilities analyst Nigel Hawkins.
But there was scepticism that other bids would follow, as The Energy Group is a unique proposition with coal interests in the United States and British generation and supply.

"Southern could be a potential target but it does not have generation or coal, while U.S. firms have already been warned off the generators," the analyst said, "the uncertainty is reflected in the share price moves."

A possible bid from U.S. group Southern for National Power was blocked around a year ago by the former Conservative government which vetoed any takeover of the privatised generators until supply and generation markets were fully competitive.

Energy Group, demerged from publicly-quoted conglomerate Hanson in February, is Britain's fourth largest generator after it bought 6,000 megaWatts of capacity from National Power and PowerGen to satisfy competition authorities.
Its supply unit, Eastern Electricity, was one of the 12 Recs set up at privatisation by the former Conservative government and bought by Hanson in September 1995.
It also owns the U.S. coal business Peabody Resources Ltd.
Analysts said there was scant reason on competition or regulatory grounds for the new Labour government to block a takeover.
"I can't see any obvious problems for the government. The Rec has already been taken over so largely it is just a change of ownership rather than structure," the analyst said.

The new Labour government, which rolled into power with a huge majority on May 1, was critical of the former administration's willingness to pass bids for Recs and thereby threaten the ability of the regulator to make comparisons in the sector.
It has privatised utilities in its sights for a one-off tax on their excess profits, which will be a central plank of its first budget on July 2.
But analysts said because the Rec business of Eastern has already been swallowed up into The Energy Group, there could be few reasons to stop the bid.
"The government might push for some compensation to customers but there are really no regulatory or competition grounds to block the bid," the analyst said.
A flurry of bids has seen all but Southern Electric of the original Recs snapped up, many by U.S. companies eager to gain experience of operating in a liberalised, regulated market.
All of the bids, apart from two by generators National Power and PowerGen, were approved by the former Conservative government, which argued against vertical integration in the industry.

The Energy Group bought generating assets from National Power and PowerGen which had been deemed excess and damaging to competition by UK authorities, succeeding in setting up its own integrated unit.
Its business would fit well with PacifiCorp, analysts said.
"There is a very good strategic fit between the two companies, it would make a business well positioned to be a global player," said the analyst.
($ = 0.610 British Pounds)
